summary: This RFC extends the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation algorithm with Explicit Address Mappings, letting an operator define exact IPv6-to-IPv4 address pairs. This makes translation possible between arbitrary IPv6 endpoints that do not use the translation prefix and IPv4. It formally updates RFC 6145.

eli5.summary: Instead of one rule for turning every name into another language, you keep a table of exact matches for the ones that need special handling.

questions: what is an explicit address mapping table
how does eam differ from rfc 6052 translation
what is hairpinning in ip translation
subtitle: Lets an operator list exact IPv4-to-IPv6 address pairs for stateless translation instead of forcing every IPv6 host into one address format.

tldr.problem: Stateless IP/ICMP translation required every IPv6 node that talks to IPv4 to carry an IPv4-translatable IPv6 address, which is scarce, restrictive in format and costly to operate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7757 adds an Explicit Address Mapping Table of IPv4 prefix and IPv6 prefix pairs; the longest matching entry is used, and the older RFC 6052 algorithm applies when nothing matches.
tldr.outcome: Arbitrary IPv6 endpoints can now be translated to and from IPv4. The RFC also gives hairpinning rules and warns about overlapping mappings and lost checksum neutrality.

today: RFC 7757 is an Internet Standard that formally updates RFC 6145. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT, RFC 6145) says that all addresses must be translated using the algorithm in RFC 6052. This document specifies an alternative: translate addresses according to a table of Explicit Address Mappings (EAMs) configured on the translator. That removes the constraint that IPv6 nodes talking to IPv4 through SIIT must have IPv4-translatable IPv6 addresses.

The new table does not replace RFC 6052. The EAM algorithm is used only when a mapping matching the address exists; otherwise RFC 6052 is used. So one packet might have one address field translated by an EAM and the other by RFC 6052.
sections.eli5: The old way had one strict rule for every address. The new way adds a list of special cases, and the old rule still handles everything the list does not mention.

sections.title: The Problem With Translatable Addresses
sections.content:
Using IPv4-translatable IPv6 addresses is not always desirable or even possible. The RFC lists these reasons:

  • Limited availability: the number of such addresses equals the number of IPv4 addresses assigned to the SIIT function, and IPv4 addresses are scarce.
  • Restricted format: they must follow the format in Section 2.2 of RFC 6052, which is not compatible with other common formats such as the EUI-64 based addresses used by IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 4862).

An operator could instead give nodes a second, translatable address, but that brings routing complexity (separate, hard-to-aggregate routes, duplicated ACL entries) and operational complexity (applications, load balancers, clusters, monitoring and the default address selection policy of RFC 6724 all need extra work).

The RFC compares this to dual stack (RFC 4213): a secondary "stack" that must be operated separately, which increases complexity and reduces reliability.
sections.eli5: If every kid needed a second, specially shaped name just to talk to one other school, the teachers would have twice the paperwork. The RFC wants to avoid that.

sections.title: The Explicit Address Mapping Table
sections.content:
An SIIT implementation includes an EAMT, a conceptual table in which each row is an EAM. Each EAM maps between an IPv4 prefix and an IPv6 prefix, and an operator fills the table. Its columns are IPv4 Prefix and IPv6 Prefix; implementations MAY add other columns for proprietary extensions.

The prefix length MAY be omitted, in which case the implementation MUST assume 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6. An EAM's IPv4 prefix MUST have an identical or smaller number of suffix bits than its IPv6 prefix.

Unless Section 4 says otherwise, an implementation MUST translate each IP address it meets in the packet's IP headers, including headers inside ICMP errors, using the procedure below. The effect is that this algorithm replaces the requirement in RFC 6145 (Sections 4.1 and 5.1) to use RFC 6052 for the Source and Destination Address fields whenever an EAM applies.
sections.eli5: The table is a two-column list: one column has the old-style address block, the other has the new-style block it matches. You look up your address and read across.

sections.title: How an Address Is Translated
sections.content:
Going from IPv4 to IPv6, the steps are:

  1. Search the IPv4 prefix column for the entry sharing the longest common prefix with the address. Call its prefixes EAM4 and EAM6.
  2. If nothing matches, abort the EAM algorithm and translate under RFC 6145 as usual.
  3. Remove the prefix bits of EAM4, keeping the remaining suffix bits in a temporary buffer.
  4. Prepend the prefix bits of EAM6.
  5. Pad with trailing zeros up to 128 bits. The buffer is the IPv6 address.

IPv6 to IPv4 is the mirror image: match on the IPv6 prefix column, strip EAM6, prepend EAM4, and discard any trailing bits beyond 32. Only the outcome is normative, so an implementation may work differently as long as the result is the same.

For example, with the table shown here, 192.0.2.24 falls under entry 3 (192.0.2.16/28 to 2001:db8:cccc::/124) and becomes 2001:db8:cccc::8.
sections.eli5: Find the best-matching row, cut off the old start of the address, and glue on the new start from the row. Fill any gap with zeros, or trim the extra, to get the right length.

sections.title: Hairpinning of IPv6 Traffic
sections.content:
If two IPv6 nodes that are both covered by EAMs talk through the translator, the reply can bypass translation and bidirectional communication may fail. In the RFC's example, node 2001:db8:aaaa:: sends to 64:ff9b::192.0.2.2. The packet is translated, loops back, and arrives at 2001:db8:bbbb::b. But that node's reply goes straight back with source 2001:db8:bbbb::b, which differs from the destination the first node used, so it will most likely be discarded.

An SIIT implementation SHOULD include a feature that supports hairpinned IPv6 traffic, and it SHOULD be enabled by default. Two approaches are given, and an implementation MAY support both:

  • Simple hairpinning: when translating IPv4 to IPv6, the EAM algorithm MUST NOT be used for the source address of a non-error packet, for the inner destination address of an ICMPv4 error, or for the outer source address of an ICMPv4 error whose outer source equals its inner destination. Those addresses are translated per RFC 6145.
  • Intrinsic hairpinning: after translating IPv6 to IPv4, if the packet meets one of two condition sets, it MUST be translated back to IPv6 immediately, applying the simple rules, and the Hop Limit SHOULD NOT be decremented.
sections.eli5: Two friends in the same building write to each other through the post office. Without a special rule, the reply comes back with a different return address than expected, and the first friend throws it away.

sections.title: Overlaps, Checksums and Security
sections.content:
Overlapping mappings. Overlapping or identical prefixes in the EAMT may make the two translation directions asymmetric and bidirectional communication impossible. In the RFC's example, an IVI-style entry for 0.0.0.0/0 and a single exception for 198.51.100.64/32 mean that 2001:db8:ffc6:3364:4000:: goes to 198.51.100.64 but that address comes back as 2001:db8::abcd. Implementations MAY warn the operator on overlap, and MAY refuse to insert an EAM whose IPv4 or IPv6 prefix is identical to an existing one. With identical IPv6 prefixes, the behavior is unspecified.

Checksums. When an address is translated by the EAM algorithm, the translation cannot be relied upon to be checksum neutral, even with the well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96.

Security. The EAM algorithm does not introduce new security issues beyond those already discussed in Section 7 of RFC 6145.
sections.eli5: If two entries in your phone book claim the same name, calls may go to the wrong place. Also, the check numbers on the envelope may no longer add up after the swap. No new danger comes from the book itself.
